facts.statement: Epitaxial films include Si; III–V arsenides, phosphides, nitrides and antimonides (GaAs, AlGaAs, InP, GaInAsP, GaP, GaN, InGaN, InAs, InSb, GaSb…); II–VI ZnSe, ZnS and HgCdTe; and oxides, nitrides and metals.
Epitaxial Si in microelectronics: a bipolar transistor sits in an n epi layer over an n⁺ buried layer; CMOS p- and n-tubs sit in a p epi layer on a p⁺ substrate.
Epitaxial means "arranged upon": a crystalline film whose lattice continues the substrate’s.
Homoepitaxy: film and substrate are the same material (Si on Si, GaAs on GaAs).
Heteroepitaxy: film and substrate differ (silicon on sapphire, Si on SiGe for HBTs and strained Si).
The three sketches: (a) a matched epi layer, (b) a relaxed layer with misfit dislocations at the interface, (c) a strained layer.
The epi layer’s lattice constant must be close to the substrate’s, otherwise the bonds cannot stretch far enough and dislocations form.
Metamorphic growth relaxes through dislocations; pseudomorphic growth keeps every bond unbroken by straining the film: compressed in the plane and elongated vertically (for a larger film lattice).
Bandgap against lattice constant: Si 5.43 Å, 1.1 eV; GaAs 5.65 Å, 1.42 eV; Ge ≈ 5.66 Å, 0.66 eV; InP 5.87 Å, 1.35 eV; InAs 6.06 Å, 0.36 eV; InSb 6.48 Å, 0.17 eV; AlAs almost matches GaAs at 2.2 eV.
On the chart, AlAs/AlGaAs sit on GaAs’s lattice constant, and In₀.₅₃Ga₀.₄₇As and In₀.₅₂Al₀.₄₈As are lattice-matched to InP; solid lines mark direct gaps, dashed indirect.

Deposition and growth: thermodynamics (supersaturation, μS < μG) drives it; then mass transport (gas-phase diffusion), reaction kinetics (homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, radical desorption) and surface incorporation kinetics (surface diffusion of reactants and adatoms, incorporation at kinks).

Stages of film growth: (a) deposition on a terrace, (b) diffusion on the terrace, (c) island nucleation, (d) attachment at islands, (e) detachment from islands, (f) deposition on an island, (g) attachment at a step, (h) desorption.
Growth modes: Volmer–Weber (islands), Stranski–Krastanov (a wetting layer, then islands) and Frank–van der Merwe (layer by layer: ideal epitaxy).
Si epi sources: silane by pyrolysis (SiH₄ → Si + 2H₂); dichlorosilane, trichlorosilane and silicon tetrachloride by H₂ reduction; disilane. Dopant gases: diborane, phosphine, arsine.
Silicon deposition from trichlorosilane: HSiCl₃ + H₂ → Si + 3HCl.
Si epi conditions: 5–50 litres/min of gas, 900–1100 °C, 100 Torr to atmospheric.
A barrel epi reactor: wafers on a faceted susceptor heated by quartz lamps, gas in at the top and out at the bottom; HCl is the etchant; Ar, H₂ and N₂ are carriers.

Epitaxy is needed when the surface region must be more resistive than the bulk (e.g. a 3 Ω·cm layer on a 0.01 Ω·cm substrate): diffusion can lower resistivity or change type, but cannot realistically raise it.
Intentional doping uses PH₃, AsH₃ or B₂H₆; incorporation is not linear in the gas-phase dopant, and dopants change the growth rate.
Epi doping ranges: B 10¹⁶–10¹⁹ cm⁻³; As and P 10¹⁶–10²⁰ cm⁻³.
Autodoping: dopant reaching the epi layer by out-diffusion from the heavily doped substrate and by incorporation from dopant in the gas phase.
The profile falls from the substrate by solid-state out-diffusion, then flattens through a gas-phase autodoping tail to the intentional level.

Minimising autodoping: grow fast; low temperature (reduces boron autodoping, not As); seal the substrate back with lightly doped poly or LT oxide; avoid HCl etching; cap–purge–grow; reduced-pressure epitaxy (thinner boundary layer, dopants swept to the exhaust).
On the diffusivity plot As and Sb are the slowest diffusers and B, P and In the fastest.
Putting Ge into the Si lattice strains it, which increases electron mobility: NMOS effective mobility rises with substrate Ge content (x = 0.10 to 0.29).
Electron mobility at 300 K (chart): InSb about 80 000 cm²/V·s, InAs about 33 000, GaAs about 8 500, Si about 1 400.
Intel’s strained-Si transistor: gate length 0.05 µm, 1.2 nm SiO₂ gate oxide, and a silicide layer contacting the poly-Si gate.

MBE is ultra-high vacuum (base pressure < 1 × 10⁻¹³ bar): ultra-pure elements (Ga and As, 7N) are sublimated and condense on the wafer; "beam" means the atoms do not meet until they reach it, because the mean free path is so long.
MBE builds layers of different materials, each a few atoms thick, "much like a many-layered cake"; cryopumps and LN₂ cryopanels maintain the vacuum.
Collision-free beams need P < 10⁻⁴ Torr; keeping the surface clean needs P < 10⁻⁹ Torr.

An MBE growth chamber: effusion cells with shutters aimed at a heated, rotating sample block (CAR assembly), a RHEED gun and fluorescent screen, an ionisation/BEP gauge, cryopanels, and a port to the buffer chamber.
A commercial MBE system joins a substrate introduction chamber, an analysis chamber and the growth chamber, with substrates moved between them on a trolley.
On the substrate the atoms move around until they find a site to bond to; shutters turn each beam on and off; the flux is set by the effusion-cell temperature.

MBE: well-controlled UHV evaporation; low growth rate and low temperature give good thickness control, sharp (monoatomic) interfaces and negligible dopant diffusion; growth is kinetically controlled; in-situ cleaning (not etching) by low-energy inert-ion sputtering or heating; in-situ RHEED; phosphorus compounds are difficult.
The impingement rate is φ = P(2πmkT)^(−1/2) = 2.64 × 10²⁰ · P/√(MT) molecules cm⁻² s⁻¹, with P in Pa, M the molecular weight and T in K.
Growth rate = φ·(A/πL²)·(monolayer thickness)/(surface density of growth-controlling atoms), with A the crucible aperture and L its distance to the substrate.

RHEED: high-energy electrons strike the surface at a grazing angle and diffract onto a phosphor screen as streaks; grazing incidence makes it surface-specific; an atomically flat surface gives sharp streaks, a rough one a diffuse pattern.
The RHEED intensity oscillates as layers form: highest at a complete monolayer (θ = 0, 1), lowest at half coverage (θ = 0.5), so one period is one monolayer; it recovers when the shutter closes.
A TEM image of an MBE superlattice shows alternating AlGaAs and GaAs layers 15 monolayers thick.
SOI: a thin Si active layer on SiO₂; the n⁺ "bathtubs" reach down to the oxide, cutting junction capacitance to the body, so devices are faster.
Soitec makes SOI wafers by "smart cut"; IBM’s alternative is SIMOX, separation by implantation of oxygen.
facts.corrects: The slide expands SIMOX as "silicon implantation with oxide"; it stands for separation by implantation of oxygen: oxygen is implanted and annealed into a buried oxide.

facts.statement: Smart cut: thermally oxidise a Si wafer, implant hydrogen below the surface, bond it to a second substrate, split it along the hydrogen layer (mechanical strain from the implant), then flip, out-diffuse the H and polish; the Si/SiO₂ interface is high quality because the oxide is thermal.
A cross-sectional TEM of a Soitec SOI wafer: a 205 nm Si layer on 400 nm of SiO₂ over the Si bulk.
SOI CMOS isolates each transistor on the buried oxide; bulk CMOS needs p- and n-wells over a p⁺ buried layer in a p substrate.
